**J. W. Smith, Y. Alimam, G. Vedula, and M. Torlak, "A Vision Transformer Approach for Efficient Near-Field SAR Super-Resolution under Array Perturbation," *Proc. IEEE Texas Symp. Wireless & Microwave Circuits & Systems (WMCS)*, 2022.** · [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1109/WMCS55582.2022.9866326)

## The problem

Synthetic aperture radar (SAR) builds a high-resolution image by moving a radar across space, forming a synthetic aperture far larger than the physical antenna and coherently combining the returns. At millimeter-wave (mmWave) frequencies — tens of GHz, wavelengths of a few millimeters — this yields optical-like resolution that can see through clothing, cardboard, and packaging. Reconstructing the image, though, requires knowing exactly where the radar was at every sample.

In a lab that's easy: precision motion stages place the antennas to within microns. But the interesting new applications can't afford that. Freehand smartphone imaging, drone-mounted (unmanned aerial vehicle, UAV) SAR, and automotive SAR all scan along trajectories whose positions must be *estimated* — by a camera-based tracker, for example — rather than commanded. Those estimates carry error. We call the resulting jitter in the assumed element locations **array perturbation**.

Position error is poison for SAR. The efficient Fourier-based reconstruction algorithms compute matched-filter weights from the assumed antenna positions; feed them noisy positions and the matched filter is wrong, so the image **defocuses and distorts**. The fast, FFT-friendly range migration algorithm (RMA) is cheap enough for a mobile device — its complexity is $O(N^2 \log N)$ — but under perturbation it produces only medium-fidelity images. The back-projection algorithm (BPA) is the gold standard and works for any geometry, but its $O(N^4)$ cost is prohibitive on the edge, and it too degrades under position error. Existing perturbation-compensation methods exist but assume far-field conditions, few scatterers, and large compute. Recovering high-fidelity images cheaply, under realistic position error, was an open problem.

## The idea

Rather than fix the radar physics, we fix the *picture*. We treat the defocused RMA output as a degraded image and learn a mapping back to a clean one — a super-resolution and artifact-mitigation problem in the image domain.

The twist is the architecture. Prior deep-learning work on SAR super-resolution was entirely convolutional neural network (CNN) based. We instead use a **vision transformer (ViT)** — the attention-based architecture that has overtaken CNNs in computer vision — adapted for mobile deployment. The result, **Mobile-SRViT**, is, to our knowledge, the first transformer-based approach for SAR image enhancement. Working in the image domain (on the reconstructed RMA image rather than the raw radar signals) is what keeps it cheap: the heavy lifting of reconstruction is already done by the efficient RMA, and the network just restores quality. That makes it suitable for edge and Internet-of-Things (IoT) devices, exactly the platforms these 5G mmWave applications target.

## How it works

The pipeline is simple. Raw multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) radar data are preprocessed into an equivalent virtual planar monostatic array, the RMA reconstructs a low-resolution image with blur and defocusing, and Mobile-SRViT maps that image to a high-fidelity output.

The network is built on the MobileViT design, converted from a classifier into a fully convolutional neural network (FCNN) for image-to-image work. It interleaves MobileNetV2 ("MV2") convolution blocks with MobileViT blocks. Each MobileViT block models both local and global structure: given an input tensor $X \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times C}$, it applies a $3\times3$ then a $1\times1$ convolution, unfolds the result into $N = HW/4$ non-overlapping patches of size $P=4$, and runs a transformer over each patch group to encode inter-patch relationships, $X_G(p) = \text{Transformer}(X_U(p))$. Unlike a standard ViT, MobileViT preserves patch and pixel ordering, so the result folds cleanly back to spatial form, gets concatenated with the input, and is fused by a final $3\times3$ convolution. The effective receptive field is the full $H \times W$.

We keep $C=16$ channels until the last block ($C=32$), use $d=2C$, depths $L=\{2,4,3\}$, $256\times256$ images, and $16\times16$ patches. The whole model is only **69,122 parameters**. Training minimizes a pixel-to-pixel L1 loss, $L_{p2p} = \lVert X_{SR} - X_{HR}\rVert_1$.

We trained for 50 epochs with ADAM on a single RTX 3090, using 4096 training and 1024 evaluation samples. A 77 GHz frequency-modulated continuous-wave (FMCW) radar with 4 GHz bandwidth and 64 ADC samples is assumed. Crucially, the training data are *realistically corrupted*: each sample gets additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) at a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) in $[-10, 50]$ dB, plus position errors with standard deviation $\sigma_\epsilon = 1$ mm in $x$, $y$, and $z$ — so the network learns to undo perturbation rather than ignore it. Training took about 6 hours; inference is **10 ms per sample**.

## Results

On a 1024-sample held-out test set, Mobile-SRViT beats both classical algorithms on every metric (best in bold):

| Metric | Mobile-SRViT | BPA | RMA |
|---|---|---|---|
| PSNR (dB) | **37.61** | 28.73 | 27.94 |
| SSIM | **0.9909** | 0.9684 | 0.9619 |
| Time (s) | **1.113** | 1324.8 | 1.103 |

The headline is that Mobile-SRViT outperforms even the gold-standard BPA — by nearly **9 dB** of peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) and on structural similarity (SSIM) — while running at essentially RMA speed: **1.113 s** total (RMA reconstruction plus the network) versus **1324.8 s** for the BPA, a roughly **1000x** speedup. Timings were measured on a 12-core AMD Ryzen 9 3900X with 64 GB of memory.

On individual synthetic samples the gains are stark: the RMA's 27.32 dB becomes 37.79 dB after Mobile-SRViT, and 24.34 dB becomes 35.31 dB. The network recovers both solid objects and point scatterers, producing images close to ground truth where the RMA gives only medium fidelity. We also stress-tested generalization: although trained only at $\sigma_\epsilon = 1$ mm, the method stays competitive against the BPA and RMA across perturbations from 1 mm up to 6 mm — degrading only once the array is perturbed enough to push the reconstructed image fully out of focus. Finally, we validated on empirical data from a real near-field SAR scan with array perturbations, where Mobile-SRViT both sharpened the image and suppressed the multistatic artifacts visible in the RMA result.

## Why it matters

This work shows you can get *better-than-gold-standard* SAR image quality at the cost of the cheapest reconstruction algorithm, on real hardware-grade position errors, with a model small enough for a phone. By doing the restoration in the image domain on top of the fast RMA, Mobile-SRViT sidesteps the compute wall that makes BPA and parametric perturbation-compensation methods infeasible on the edge. That unlocks the applications driving near-field mmWave sensing — freehand smartphone scanners, UAV SAR, and automotive imaging — where precision positioning hardware simply isn't available. And because the approach treats imaging non-idealities as an image-restoration task, the same recipe could plausibly tackle other SAR distortions, from clock-synchronization errors to chirp nonlinearity, given the right synergy between signal processing and deep learning.
